extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / literate early-18th-century public interested in morals, manners, and literature
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and critical criteria embedded in Spectator essays about moral instruction, marriage manners, character (female virtues), authorship in old age, and qualities of epic poetry. The page offers prescriptive guidance for behaviour and aesthetic judgement rather than a formal rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral instruction via exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: It is observed, that a Man improves more by reading the Story of a Person eminent for Prudence and Virtue, than by the finest Rules and Precepts of Morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer teaching by narrative example (stories of virtuous/prudent persons) rather than by abstract maxims; present a case and allow readers to draw lessons rather than over-explaining with additional reflections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in public behaviour of married couples
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposes finding a mean between being Wasps and Doves in Publick: avoid being constantly quarreling or ostentatiously affectionate; avoid making 'nauseous Allusions to private Familiarities' before company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage discretion: couples should not perform extremes of affection or sharp wit in mixed company. If couples display continuous public fondness or provocative banter they produce discomfort in observers; recommend sincere, stable feelings rather than theatrical behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intimate or indecent talk in mixed company
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticises those (e.g., 'Lucina') who 'talks with a very grave Air in such a Manner, as is very improper so much as to be hinted at' before virgins and general company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from discussing medical/sexual/private subjects in public or before the young; discretion in topics preserves decorum and spares observers embarrassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarding the innocent from flattery and false addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Young or raw women (and their parents) are to be blamed if they fall to false addresses; those who ought to hinder men from opportunities of imposition should not promote or encourage them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility rests with guardians and with mature women to protect the inexperienced; prevent situations encouraging imposition and flattery; question social enablers who privately profit from such exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to treat inconstant friendship (valetudinary friendship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describes the common fault of affected strangeness and coldness in those who formerly showed civility; asks how one must behave toward a friendship subject to 'Heats and Colds'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While less prescriptive than other items, the implied guidance is to diagnose and address shifting civility rather than immediately assuming offence—consider causes and respond with temperate behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admired female character: beauty united with wisdom and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘There is nothing which gives one so pleasing a Prospect of human Nature, as the Contemplation of Wisdom and Beauty.... As therefore Virtue makes a beautiful Woman appear more beautiful, so Beauty makes a virtuous Woman really more virtuous.’ (Character of Emilia.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valorise a combination of natural charm and steady moral qualities: unstudied graces, modesty, decency that reins in licentious impulses, consistent piety and compassionate reason—virtue should be visible in uniform conduct rather than ostentatious or theatrical devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marital management by example and attention to small things
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Her Ingenuity has been constantly employed in humanizing his Passions... a silent Example and an easie unrepining Behaviour, will always be more perswasive than the Severity of Lectures and Admonitions.’ Also: neglect of apparel (wrapping gowns and dirty linen) is ‘the Bane of conjugal Love’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In marriage, use gentle, practical management—lead by example and mild artifice rather than harsh remonstrance; attend to seemingly trivial matters (clean, decent dress, small attentions) because they materially affect affection and respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should adapt to age and not rely on past accomplishments
rubrics_metrics.description: We are so much pleased with little Accomplishments that have made us remarkable, that we endeavour to persuade ourselves it is not in the Power of Time to rob us of them... an Author writes on, tho he is come to Dotage, without considering that his Memory is impaired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors (and people generally) should recognise diminished faculties with age and avoid continuing past methods or public postures that no longer suit them; avoid producing work in dotage that merely repeats earlier successes—adapt style and subject to present capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate invocation in epic poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's 'Invocation to a Work which turns in a great measure upon the Creation of the World, is very properly made to the Muse who inspired Moses ... and to the Holy Spirit'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When beginning an epic or grand poem, address a muse or spiritual authority suitable to the poem's subject-matter (e.g., using the Muse associated with sources or traditions the poem draws upon) so the exordium feels natural and authoritative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plainness and simplicity where appropriate (conformity to Homer and Horace)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘These Lines are perhaps as plain, simple and unadorned as any of the whole Poem, in which Particular the Author has conformed himself to the Example of Homer and the Precept of Horace.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value clarity and unadorned diction in key passages; restraint can be a virtue and align with classical precepts—balance ornament with plain expression where the subject calls for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noble language and sentiment, and natural transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘This whole Exordium rises very happily into noble Language and Sentiment, as I think the Transition to the Fable is exquisitely beautiful and natural.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for elevated diction and sentiment in grand poetry, and ensure transitions (exordium → fable) are smooth and feel organically motivated rather than forced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention of striking, noble circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Praises the 'Nine Days Astonishment' (angels entranced) as a 'noble Circumstance' and instances such as the division of Hell into seas of fire and firm ground and exclusion of Hope as 'great and fruitful Invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create imaginative, striking set-pieces and structural conceits that deepen the poem's moral and emotional effects; original, vivid circumstances elevate the work and engage the reader's imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: World-building: coherent original cosmology or locale
rubrics_metrics.description: Commends Milton's 'Division of Hell into Seas of Fire, and into firm Ground impregnated with the same furious Element' and particularities such as 'the Exclusion of Hope'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting other realms, build coherent and memorable rules/structures that enhance the poem's thematic force—distinctive, internally consistent features (like the exclusion of hope) make the setting convincing and affective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powerful, complex characterization of principal antagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The Thoughts in the first Speech and Description of Satan... are wonderfully proper to give us a full Idea of him. His Pride, Envy and Revenge, Obstinacy, Despair and Impenitence, are all of them very artfully interwoven.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce major antagonists with speeches/descriptions that concentrate and intertwine their chief passions and contradictions—this compels empathy and terror and clarifies moral stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use incidents to raise and terrify the reader's imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The whole part of this great Enemy of Mankind is filled with such Incidents as are very apt to raise and terrifie the Readers Imagination.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ vivid incidents and scenes that provoke strong imaginative/emotional responses (terror, awe) appropriate to the subject; pacing and incident selection should aim to move the reader deeply, not merely to instruct.
